title: Bike Lane Pilot Brief
topic: A year-long comparison of a new protected lane
blurb: The city circulated this note after a year of the new lane.
prompt: The city circulated this note after a year of the new bike lane. Tap any line that doesn't hold up, or mark it clean.

segments.label: The window
segments.text: The city installed a protected bike lane on Oak Avenue and tracked weekday traffic for 12 full months before and 12 months after.

segments.label: The comparison
segments.text: Over the same period, planners also watched Pine Avenue — a nearby commercial street with similar traffic that did not get a bike lane.

segments.label: The cycling change
segments.text: Daily bike trips rose 35% on Oak Avenue versus only 5% on Pine Avenue, a roughly 30-point gain beyond citywide seasonal trends.

segments.label: The shop question
segments.text: Card-payment totals along Oak Avenue stayed essentially flat (+1.2% vs +0.9% on Pine), rather than relying only on informal merchant surveys.

segments.label: The scope
segments.text: The pilot supports a net rise in cycling on flat commercial streets like Oak Avenue, though steeper or suburban roads may behave differently.

conclusion: City verdict: After a controlled year-long comparison, cycling rose on Oak Avenue without a measurable hit to card sales, with the limits of that claim spelled out.
clean_segments: The city installed a protected bike lane on Oak Avenue and tracked weekday traffic for 12 full months before and 12 months after.
Over the same period, planners also watched Pine Avenue — a nearby commercial street with similar traffic that did not get a bike lane.
Daily bike trips rose 35% on Oak Avenue versus only 5% on Pine Avenue, a roughly 30-point gain beyond citywide seasonal trends.
Card-payment totals along Oak Avenue stayed essentially flat (+1.2% vs +0.9% on Pine), rather than relying only on informal merchant surveys.
The pilot supports a net rise in cycling on flat commercial streets like Oak Avenue, though steeper or suburban roads may behave differently.
clean_conclusion: The write-up uses a full-year window, a matched control street, actual card sales instead of vibes, and a carefully scoped conclusion.

diagnosis: Tracking only weekday traffic drops weekend leisure riders and exaggerates the commuting jump.
12 months before and 12 months after is still too short because bike-lane habits take 3 years to stabilize.
Measuring Oak Avenue alone without checking parallel car lanes misses traffic spillover onto side streets.
Counting trips instead of unique riders double-counts the same commuters riding twice a day.
fix: Include Saturday and Sunday bike counts before calling it a full-year comparison.
Extend the pilot to 36 months so novelty effects wear off.
Measure car congestion on nearby residential side streets too.
Track unique cyclists via survey instead of total daily bike trips.

diagnosis: Because Pine Avenue is nearby, cyclists simply shifted from Pine to Oak, inflating Oak's +35% gain.
A single control street can't control for citywide trends — you need at least ten matched avenues.
Pine Avenue didn't get construction, so comparing it to Oak misses the disruption period.
Having 'similar traffic' beforehand doesn't mean Pine had the same share of cyclists.
fix: Pick a control street in a different district so riders can't migrate from Pine to Oak.
Average five or more control corridors instead of relying on Pine Avenue alone.
Exclude the first three months after construction from both Oak and Pine.
Verify Pine Avenue's baseline bike volume before comparing percentage jumps.

diagnosis: Subtracting 5% from 35% to get a 30-point gain is invalid because Oak and Pine started from different base counts.
35% vs 5% is a 7× relative gain, not a 30-point gain — you mixed up ratio and subtraction.
A 35% jump on a tiny baseline (say 20 bikes/day) is only 7 extra bikes, which could be pure noise.
Comparing percentage changes without reporting the raw trip counts hides whether cycling actually rose meaningfully.
fix: Report raw daily bike counts on both streets instead of subtracting percentages.
Divide 35% by 5% to express the relative multiplier instead of 30 points.
Check whether Oak Avenue started from a tiny base before calling 35% substantial.
Adjust for weather differences between the two 12-month windows first.

diagnosis: Card-payment totals ignore cash sales, which are a huge share of small corner shops along Oak Avenue.
+1.2% vs +0.9% doesn't adjust for inflation — in real terms, shop revenue fell on both streets.
A 0.3-point gap (+1.2% vs +0.9%) is too small to be statistically significant, so it proves nothing.
Card totals pool big chains with mom-and-pop stores, hiding heavy losses at small shops.
fix: Include cash register receipts alongside card totals before clearing the bike lane.
Subtract annual inflation (~3%) so you report real sales rather than nominal totals.
Break out independent shops separately from national chains along Oak Avenue.
Run a merchant profit survey to verify whether parking loss hurt margins.

diagnosis: Claiming a 'net rise in cycling' assumes riders didn't just detour off Pine Avenue onto Oak Avenue.
Limiting the claim to flat commercial streets makes the pilot useless for the rest of the city.
One year of flat card sales (+1.2%) isn't enough to call the lane harmless without checking store closures.
This jumps from correlation (lane installed + more bikes) to causation without randomizing which street got the lane.
fix: Narrow the conclusion to 'trips on Oak rose' without claiming a citywide net rise.
Check shop turnover and vacancy rates over the 12 months before concluding zero hit.
Randomly assign bike lanes to half of the city's commercial streets before concluding causation.
Wait for a second post-installation year before recommending lanes on similar flat streets.

explanation: The write-up uses a full-year window, a matched control street, actual card sales instead of vibes, and a carefully scoped conclusion.
